name: CSRF and CORS
intent: Understand what browsers send and allow across websites: stop other sites from making your logged-in users act without knowing, and open cross-origin access only to origins you choose.
scenario: A user is logged in to a bank in one tab and visits a harmless-looking page in another. That page quietly submits a hidden form to the bank. Because browsers attach cookies automatically, the bank sees a request from the real, logged-in user.
problem: Browsers attach a site's cookies to every request to that site, no matter which page triggered it. So any website can make a user's browser send authenticated requests to your server (cross-site request forgery). Meanwhile a separate browser rule, the same-origin policy, stops one site from reading another's responses, and CORS is how a server deliberately relaxes that rule. The two are often confused.

howItWorks.title: CSRF: the browser sends the cookie for you
howItWorks.text: A request to bank.example carries the bank's session cookie even when it was started by evil.example. The bank cannot tell it from a real click unless it checks something an outside site cannot supply. State-changing endpoints (transfers, password changes, deletions) are the targets.

howItWorks.title: Defence 1: SameSite cookies
howItWorks.text: Setting SameSite=Lax (the default in modern browsers) or Strict tells the browser not to send the cookie on cross-site POST requests and subresource loads. Strict also withholds it on links from other sites; Lax allows top-level GET navigation only. SameSite=None sends it everywhere and must be paired with other defences.

howItWorks.title: Defence 2: anti-CSRF tokens and origin checks
howItWorks.text: The server includes a random, per-session token in its own pages and requires it in every state-changing request (in a hidden field or header). An attacking page cannot read the token, so it cannot include it. Servers can also verify that the Origin or Referer header names their own site.

howItWorks.title: The same-origin policy: you may send, but not read
howItWorks.text: A page can usually send a request to another origin, but the browser will not let its script read the response. An origin is scheme plus host plus port. This protects the data in responses (a different problem from forged requests).

howItWorks.title: CORS: a server opts in to sharing
howItWorks.text: A server can send headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin to allow specific origins to read its responses. For requests that could have side effects (JSON bodies, custom headers, PUT and DELETE) the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request and proceeds only if the server agrees. CORS is a browser-enforced permission, not an access control: it does not stop curl or a malicious server, and it is not a CSRF defence.

pros: SameSite cookies stop most CSRF with one setting and no code
CSRF tokens work in every browser and for every cookie policy
The same-origin policy protects response data by default
CORS lets you share an API with chosen sites without opening it to all
cons: Each defence covers only part of the problem, so they are usually combined
CSRF tokens need server state or signing, and care with single-page apps
CORS misconfiguration (allowing every origin, or reflecting the Origin header) leaks data
SameSite behaviour has edge cases across browsers and with embedded or cross-site flows
whenToUse: CSRF defences on every endpoint that changes state and relies on cookie authentication
CORS only when a browser app on another origin genuinely needs your API
whenNotToUse: CSRF tokens for APIs that use an Authorization header with a bearer token the browser does not attach on its own
Wildcard CORS (*) on endpoints that return private data, and never with credentials
pitfalls: Treating CORS as protection against forged requests or against non-browser clients
Reflecting any incoming Origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with credentials enabled
Allowing state changes through GET requests
Setting SameSite=None 'to make it work' without adding a token or origin check
